name: Hassan Petrov

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Is that all right?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Yes, fine. I'll try to be straight with you. I'm not against technology, I just like to see it work first.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Good. Can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for one of the big national home care companies, on a patch of suburbs on the south side of the city. Most of my calls are double-ups, which means two carers, because the clients need a hoist: stroke patients, a man with MS, a lady with a bad hip. I'm paired most days with Grace, who's been doing it fifteen years and still corrects how I fold the sling. I do about nine calls a day in my own car, and I write the notes on the company phone afterwards. I like the lifting work, I'm strong and I'm careful, but I left school early and I'm still slow on the medication side. What wears me out is the evening shifts, because Lena, my fiancée, works days and we barely see each other.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay. Honestly, I'd half expect that. Lots of noise, small change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it like it is: it helped a bit with the rota, but carers still do the work. I wouldn't post anything, I'm not big online. With friends I'd probably joke that the robots aren't coming for my hoist.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means we keep saving for the wedding and the deposit the slow way. Lena works in an insurance call centre and I'm on care pay, so it's tight, and we've got about three months put by. The company also changes the rota every few weeks, so my hours jump around and some weeks I'm short.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going, save what I can, and finish the medication training so I can do solo calls, which pay a bit better. I'd also look at the moving-and-handling trainer course the company advertises, because I'm good at lifting. And we'd set the wedding for next autumn, small, family only.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay. A bit stretched, but okay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said some weeks you're short of hours. How short?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some weeks I get 32 hours instead of 38. That's most of the weekly shop. When it happens two weeks running, we dip into the savings, and then Lena gets stressed about the deposit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the one thing you'd change about the job if you could?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Guaranteed hours. Not more money even, just knowing what's coming. You can't plan a wedding on a rota that changes every fortnight.

say: AI helped a bit with the **rota**, but carers still do the work.
I'd joke with friends that robots aren't coming for **my hoist**.
think: We'd keep saving for the **wedding and deposit** the slow way.
My **hours jump around**, and short weeks mean dipping into savings.
do: Finish the **medication training** to qualify for better-paid solo calls.
Look at the company's **moving-and-handling trainer** course.
Set a **small wedding** for next autumn.
S0.quote: You can't plan a wedding on a rota that changes every fortnight.
fieldNote: Pressure comes from **unstable hours**, not AI.
Wants **guaranteed hours** more than a pay rise.
Sees his **lifting skill** as a route to a trainer role.

steps.text: Finish the medication training for solo calls
Hold a small family-only wedding next autumn
Keep three months saved toward a flat deposit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thinking tasks first. Answering customers. That's Lena's job, straight away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say carers are fine, it's the office and call centres that get hit. I'd tell my friends to learn the tools if they're at a desk. I'd keep it practical, no drama.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm not worried about me, I'm worried about Lena. My fiancée's call centre is basically answering customers and checking claims, which is exactly that list. If her team shrinks, we go from two incomes to one and a half, and the deposit gets pushed back years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit down with Lena this month and work out the budget on one income, just in case. I'd push to finish the medication training quicker so I can do solo calls. I'd start using the AI notes tool once Grace and the others have tried it, because it would save me twenty minutes an evening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy for me, properly anxious for us. Those are different things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut first, if Lena's hours went?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The car upgrade I was looking at, and the honeymoon. We'd still get married, just at the registry and a meal after. My mum would be disappointed, but she'd get over it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And what would Lena do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She's said she might train as a dental receptionist or something with patients. I'd support that. We'd probably move the wedding back a year so she could pay for a course.

say: Carers are fine; it's **offices and call centres** that get hit.
People at desks should **learn the tools**, no drama.
think: My fiancée's **call centre** job is exactly on that list.
Two incomes become **one and a half**, and the deposit slips years.

Finish the **medication training** sooner for solo calls.
Use the AI **notes tool** once colleagues have tested it.
feel: **Uneasy** for himself, but properly **anxious** for the household.
S1.quote: My fiancée's call centre is basically answering customers and checking claims, which is exactly that list.
fieldNote: The threat lands on his **fiancée's job**, which is high on thinking AI.
He separates his own **safe hands-on** work from the household's risk.
Would shrink the **wedding** and delay it to fund her retraining.

steps.text: Draw up a one-income budget with his fiancée this month
Try AI voice care notes once his colleagues have tested them
Move the wedding back a year to fund her course

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2028 Lena's job is gone. And by 2031 robots doing my hoist calls. That's both of us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need a proper plan from the government, some income support while people retrain, because whole families get hit at once. At work I'd keep my head down. I'd not want to scare the newer carers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think this is the bad one for us. Lena loses her job in the first year or two, and I've got three more years before robots can do double-up hoist calls cheaper than two carers. Two carers on one call is exactly what a company would replace first, because it's double the cost.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight away, I'd stop all wedding spending and put everything into savings, aiming for six months. I'd take every extra shift I could get in 2027 while the money's there. I'd look at work where people want a person in the room, maybe a hospital porter or patient transport, and get Lena onto a course with whatever help there was.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be the one trying to sound calm at home and then sitting in the car for ten minutes before going in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said double-up calls would go first. Why do you think that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the company pays two of us for one job. If one robot can do the hoist and one carer stays for checking, they halve the cost overnight. I'd be the junior one, so I'd be the one that goes, not Grace.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to the wedding?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd postpone it. Lena says she'd rather wait than start married with nothing. We'd still live together, nothing changes there, just no party.

say: Government needs a plan with **income support** while families retrain.
At work I'd **keep my head down** and not scare newer carers.
think: My fiancée loses her job early, and robots reach **double-up hoist calls** by 2031.
As the **junior** on a double-up, I'd be the one cut, not my senior colleague.
do: Stop all **wedding spending** and aim for six months saved.
Take every **extra shift** in 2027 while work is there.
Look at **porter or patient transport** roles and fund his fiancée's course.
feel: **Alarmed**, sounding calm at home but sitting in the car before going in.
S2.quote: Two carers on one call is exactly what a company would replace first, because it's double the cost.
fieldNote: Both household jobs fall on **different dates**, 2028 for hers and 2031 for his.
He reads his **double-up calls** as the first target for cost cutting.
Hides his fear at home: **ten minutes** in the car before going in.

steps.text: Pause all wedding spending and save toward six months
Take every extra shift on offer in 2027
Apply for hospital porter or patient transport jobs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years, robots around 2034. Lena's job still goes first, but we'd have time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say with five years there's no excuse for families being left with nothing. I'd tell friends at desks to retrain now, while they're still earning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think we'd get through it if we use the time. Lena would have years to train for something with patients. I'd have until about 2034, and by then I could be the moving-and-handling trainer or something that teaches people and checks the machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year, I'd do the medication training and apply for the trainer course. I'd get Lena to start her course in the evenings in 2027 while she still has the call centre wage. We'd still get married next autumn, but smaller, and keep saving for the deposit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with a plan. It's like a long drive where you know the road.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be a trainer. Would trainers still be needed once robots do the lifting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fair question. For a few years, yes, someone has to show families and carers how it works. After that, I don't know. I'd want to be using AI tools by then too, once everyone else is, so I'm not the one left behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your mum about the wedding?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her we're doing it, but not the big hall. She wanted a hundred people. We'd do forty guests instead of the big hall and spend the rest on my fiancée's course.

Friends at desks should **retrain now** while still earning.
think: We'd **get through it** if we use the time well.
By 2034 I could be a **moving-and-handling trainer** who also checks machines.
do: Finish **medication training** and apply for the trainer course this year.
Have his fiancée start an **evening course** in 2027 while earning.
Keep a **smaller wedding** next autumn and keep saving.
feel: **Anxious** but with a **plan**, like a long drive on a known road.
S3.quote: We'd do forty guests instead of the big hall and spend the rest on my fiancée's course.
fieldNote: Five years turns the household crisis into a **two-step plan**.
Admits a **trainer role** may only last a few years after robots arrive.
Would follow colleagues into **AI tools** so as not to be left behind.

steps.text: Apply for the company's moving-and-handling trainer course
Fund his fiancée's evening course from 2027
Hold a forty-guest wedding and save the difference
Pick up AI tools once his colleagues use them

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, robots in 2039. I'd be nearly 40. We'd probably have kids by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's enough time if people start early, and I'd mean it. With friends, I'd say it's the one I can live with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd feel safe for the first few years. Lena would have time to move into something with patients, and I'd have over a decade in care. The worry would be kids, because by 2039 I'd be the one with a mortgage and children and a job a robot can do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd get married next autumn as planned. I'd do the medication and trainer courses over the next two years, and start using AI tools once they're normal at work. We'd try to buy a flat by 2030 so we're not renting when the change comes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm, a bit of unease in the background.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd buy a flat by 2030. Isn't that a risk if your job goes in 2039?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. But renting at 40 with kids and no job is worse than any mortgage. At least with a flat we'd have something, and nine years of payments behind us. We'd keep a big cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about at work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Grace, honestly. She's 54 and she'd be 66 by then, so she might just retire. It's the carers in their forties I'd worry about, the ones with kids now.

say: Ten years is **enough time** if people start early.
Among the five pictures, this is the one I **can live with**.
think: I'd feel **safe** for the first few years.
By 2039 I'd have a **mortgage and children** and a job a robot can do.
do: Finish **medication and trainer** courses over two years.
Aim to **buy a flat** by 2030 and keep a big cushion.
feel: **Mostly calm**, with some unease in the background.
S4.quote: Renting at 40 with kids and no job is worse than any mortgage.
fieldNote: Plans a **flat purchase** as protection, not as a gamble.
Worries about carers in their **forties with kids**, not the older ones near retirement.
Ten years lets the **wedding go ahead** on time.

steps.text: Marry next autumn as originally planned
Complete medication and trainer courses over two years
Buy a flat with his fiancée by 2030

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it hits both of us, Lena first and then me three years later. What would help is income support while people retrain, and a clear date from the company about when the double-up calls change, so I'm not guessing.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about couples. Everyone asks about one person's job. In our house it's two jobs and one deposit, and the timing matters more than anything.

headlineQuote: In our house it's two jobs and one deposit, and the timing matters more than anything.
portrait: A 27-year-old care worker at a **national company**, doing double-up hoist calls in the suburbs.
Left school early, strong and careful, but **slow on medication** and still training.
Engaged to a **call centre worker**, whose job is far more exposed than his.
Steady and practical: tries tools **once colleagues have**, and plans with budgets.
Most alarmed in **AGI by 2028**, when both household jobs fall within three years.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, which hits his fiancée first and then his double-up calls.
whatWouldHelp: A clear **company date** for when double-up calls change.
